title: WARDS SILK FACTORY
description: Wards Silk Factory. Built between 1792 and 1807 for silk throwing. 2 storeys, rubble stone range of 7 bays with a 2 bay extension to the west end and a three bay extension to the east end. The windows have very shallow segmental brick heads, brick jambs, stone sills and modern wooden frames. The roof of the east-west range including the extensions is covered with red tiles which may be original. By 1867 a 4 bay wing was added at right angles to the northern end, this wing has a loading door in the gable facing the road. The eastern elevation has a slate roof while the western elevation has a corrugated asbestos roof. The first storey windows on the eastern side of the wing are blocked. The first storey windows in the western elevation are glazed. The ground floor has wide modern sliding doors and a corrugated asbestos roof. A further 2 bay wing had been added to the northern side of the western extension by 1867, this linked what may have been the overseer's cottage to the mill. The western extension to the factory is in domestic use. On the west side of the road is a rubble built mill of 3 storeys and 10 bays. This mill was built circa 1861 by James and William Kemp for weaving silk velvet. The windows have ashlar surrounds, all the openings facing the road have been infilled. A single bay extension at the north end has an inserted window above and a blocked door below.

title: SILK MILLS
description: On the north side of the street are the ruined walls of a small water-powered mill, with stone-mullioned window at low level onto road, probably of 18th century date. To the west is 2 storey early 18th century occupied house. To the west again is an imposing 18th century owner's house of 3 storeys and 7 bays. Up the slope to the north is a large derelict ivy-covered rubble building, probably built in the early 19th century, with 2-light casements with wooden frames and lintels to the south, possible with an integral chimney in the southwest corner, and a broad stone-arched doorway to the east. On the south side of the street is an early-mid 19th century rubble stone workshop block of 3 storeys and 4 bays under a tiled roof, this has now been converted to a dwelling. There are 2 ashlar doorways and, on each of the 2nd and 3rd storeys, 2 and 3 light square stone mullioned windows and a loading door (now glazed).

title: Site of First World War National Aircraft Factory No. 3, later British Enka Artificial Silk Company factory, Aintree
description:
Former site of First World War National Aircraft Factory No. 3, later British Enka Artificial Silk Company factory, Aintree. (1)
The National Aircraft Factory No. 3 was founded in 1917 and operated by Cunard. It was tasked with producing Bristol F.2 Fighters for the new Royal Air Force. A total of 126 aircraft were built by the end of the war in November 1918. The work was carried out by women. (2)
The factory was served by a rail line running along an embankment and over a bridge over the Ormskirk Road, visible in aerial photographs of 1928. (3)
The site is censored on the 3rd edition 25" OS map of 1927. The factory, rail link and bridge are not shown, but the spur off from the railway to the edge of Ormskirk Road is shown.
The British Enka Artificial Silk Company acquired the site as a UK factory base in 1927. In 1961 the company was sold to Courtaulds who closed it in 1981. It was involved in the manufacturing of synthetic fabrics. (4)
A second rail link was constructed in the 1960s, further to the south, the embankment and bridge of which remain.
The site was redeveloped in the 1980s as a retail park.

title: Historic Building Recording at No.64 Tredegar Road, Tower Hamlets, London, E3 2EP
description: Pre-Construct Archaeology Limited was commissioned to carry out building recording of buildings at 64 Tredegar Road, Bow, London Borough of Tower Hamlets. The work was required as a condition of planning permission for the demolition of the existing buildings and the erection of new residential units. A former silk mill on the site was recorded in accordance with English Heritage Level 3, while the other buildings were recorded in accordance with Level 1.   The earliest dated building on the site was the former silk mill, constructed for Stephen Walters  and  Sons in 1873. Other buildings present on the site included a warehouse and an office block, both of which were built for Tilley, Carr  and  Co in the late 1940s/early 1950s.   The 1873 building was a rare example of a 19th century steam-powered silk mill, used for the manufacture of umbrella and parasol silks. Evidence of the factory's original function, including the oversized ground and first floor windows and fittings associated with the line shafting that drove the looms was recorded.  Documentary evidence indicated that manufacturing took place at the mill for less than thirty years, following which it was used as warehousing for more than a century.  Building recording revealed evidence of numerous modifications made to adapt the building to its new function, as well as repairs and reconstruction that took place after it was bombed during the Second World War.

title: Archaeological investigations at the Churnet Works, Macclesfield Road,
description: Archaeological works were undertaken on behalf of Sainsbury's Ltd at the Churnet Works,  Macclesfield Road, Leek (NGR SJ 976 571). The archaeological works consisted of evaluation, building recording and watching brief. The building recording produced a photographic survey of all twelve of the buildings on the site. These consisted of a Grade II listed 18th footbridge, part of a late 18th century silk mill and its 19th century extensions, a 19th century dye works and its 20th century extensions along the south and north banks of the River Churnet. During the evaluation two sandstone walls and a brick floor were recorded in the south-east corner of the site, relating to the 19th century dye works. During archaeological monitoring of groundworks a wooden structure measuring 6m by 1.50m was uncovered submerged in the river bed close to Brindley Mill, conjectured to date from between 1862 and 1878 and relating to activity at the Silk Mill. No other significant archaeological remains was apparent elsewhere and the majority of the works site  appears top have been truncated prior to construction of the early-mid 20th century Churnet Works buildings. Evaluation of the floodplain to the north of the site revealed a single mid 18th century field boundary ditch and a moderately deep soil sequence over alluvial clays.

title: CHURNET WORKS, MACCLESFIELD ROAD
description: A desk-based assessment was undertaken on land off Macclesfield Road, Leek, Staffordshire (NGR SJ 97727 56939). The aims of this assessment were to summarise the character and extent of any identified features of the historic environment, indicate their significance, the impact of the proposed development and identify mitigation measures, where appropriate. The town of Leek has a long held connection with the industrial production of silk, dyes and textiles. Many of the mills were located adjacent to the area which this assessment addresses, and with good reason. The site is traversed by the River Churnet which has been used, and its course modified for agricultural and industrial purposes, since medieval times. The monks of Dieulacres Abbey resided to the north of the site from as early as the 13th century. They maintained two mills through the medieval period, the exact location of which are unknown, although two were recorded during the Reformation in 1538-40 off Mill Street. In the 1740s, the river's course was manipulated to provide power to the corn mill built by the prominent canal engineer, James Brindley.A leat of probable post-medieval date crosses the site and is considered to be of importance to the town's industrial history. At the southeast entrance to the Churnet Industrial Estate a stone footbridge of 17th-18th century date straddles the river. A further 18th-19th century industrial site, to the south of the assessment area, is recorded as a mineral works, associated with the extractive industry, and survives as a brick-vaulted, rock cut chamber. There are a number of listed buildings adjacent to the site, most notably the mid 18th century Brindley Corn Mill, within the mill complex which is a scheduled ancient monument. Consideration will therefore need to be given to the visual setting of these structures which lie close to the proposed residential area. Information from OASIS Online Form.

title: Melbourne Sewers Project, Derby Road and Chapel Street Sewer Main. Melbourne, Derbyshire: Archaeological Watching Brief
description: Wessex Archaeology was commissioned by Severn Trent Water Ltd. to undertake an archaeological watching brief during site investigation works involving the monitoring of five trial pits (TP01-TP05) spread across a 630 m stretch of western Melbourne, Derbyshire. This work occurred in 2022.  In April 2023, two further trial pits (TP06-07) were monitored. These were located on land between Derby Road and Chapel Street. Between 30 MayÃ¢ÂÂ08 September 2023 a third watching brief occurred, this time on the machine-excavation of 19 ground inspection trial holes. These were dug within the south-eastern part of Melbourne, chiefly between Station Road in the north and Church Street in the south. Between 31 JulyÃ¢ÂÂ16 August 2023 groundworks within a 6 x 4 m area to the west of Chapel Street (centered NGR 438638 325439) were monitored.   In 2024 Wessex Archaeology was commissioned by Severn Trent Water to undertake an archaeological watching brief during site investigation works involving the monitoring of two trial holes (TH102, TH103) located along Blackwell Lane. The watching brief recorded the initial machine excavation of TH102. The excavation was abandoned part way through due to access issues and a need for road closure. The attending archaeologist recorded the trial hole once it had been dug.  The second stage of GI works was recorded by Severn Trent Water. This comprised the reopening and expansion of TH102 and the excavation of TH103. A record sheet containing photographs, scaled plans and descriptions of the stratigraphic sequence of each trial hole, with measurements was emailed to Wessex Archaeology in January 2025. No archaeological remains were observed within trial pits 01-05 (project code 265381). Within TP06-07, dug the following year (265382), a wall was seen. This matched the position and course of a building of probable 19th-century date recorded on historic maps. A stone surface (seen in both trial pits) to the north of the wall may have been an adjacent access road/path into the site, which the cartographic evidence indicates formed part of the ÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂKendrick Boot, Shoe and Silk MillsÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂ complex. During the watching brief on Ground Investigation works (265383), the recorded sequence in each trial hole typically comprised natural alluvial clay overlain by undated or modern made ground of uncertain derivation, service ducts and their backfills, modern preparation layers and existing road surfaces. Other remains include a surface comprising paving setts, a drain and masonry. These other remains were not formally dated but are likely to be modern (19th century +). During the 4th watching brief forming part of this project (WA proj no 265384, a 6 x 4 m area centered 438638 325439) five phases of activity were identified. All of the dated remains relate to Kendrick mills or subsequent activity on the site. Finds were sparse and no environmental samples were collected. Phase 1 relates to the natural substrate and buried soil sequence. These were cut by the foundation trenches of a building forming part of the Kendrick mills complex in the mid-19th century (phase 2). Phases 3 and 4 represent the use and then demolition of the mills complex, identified by floor surfaces overlain by rubble and made ground. Finally, phase 5 remains represent modern activity, and include a wall, service ducts and the footprint of an earlier watching brief trial hole. The excavated remains of Kendrick mills are not at odds with the cartographic evidence, and the watching brief has provided further, albeit limited, detail on the appearance and internal layout of the buildings, and the methods and materials used in their construction. The fifth phase of monitoring took place at Melbourne Hall Tea Rooms.

title: Site of William Earle's house, Netherfield Road North, Everton
description:
Former site of William Earle's house, Netherfield Road North, Everton.
No building is shown in this area on Yates and Perry's map of 1768. (1)
Horwood's plan of 1803 shows a large house on this site and labels it William Earle. (2)
Bennison's map of 1835 shows the building and labels it W. Earle. (3)
The building is shown on the OS town plan of 1850.
William Earle (1760-1839), a Liverpool merchant, magistrate, deputy lieutenant and colonel of the Liverpool fusiliers, lived in a large mansion on Netherfield Road at Everton. He bought the property from G. Slater. He did not live at the house left to him by his father in his will, proved in 1790. (4)
A map of 1865 shows houses across this area. (5)
William Earle was a partner with his brother, Thomas, in T. and W. Earle and Company, merchants trading in iron, wine, oil, silk, sugar and slaves. The Earles were the tenth largest British slave traders and the second largest at Calabar and the Cameroons. They were also slave owners, acquiring a plantation in Berbice, British Guiana in the 1830s. In addition, they also had interests in privateers. (6)

title: An Assessment of an Archaeological Monitoring Exercise on Land at 72-78 Conington Road, Lewisham, London SE13
description: An archaeological watching brief was undertaken by Pre-Construct Archaeology Ltd on land at 72 - 78 Conington Road between the 11th of June and the 18th of July 2007. The earliest deposit encountered on the site took the form of the natural Upper Chalk. This chalk was overlain by the Ravensbourne Gravels which in turn were sealed with alluvial deposits associated with the River Ravensbourne. A sub square brick structure was also discovered and is believed to have related to repairs and improvements that took place to the armoury mill in 1754. The main phase of archaeological activity related to the discovery of the Royal Armoury Mill building, which was constructed in 1807. This was converted into a silk mill in 1824 and finally demolished between 1937 and 1938.

title: Desk-Based Assessment of the Churnet Works, Macclesfield Road, Leek, Staffordshire
description: A desk-based assessment was undertaken on land off Macclesfield Road, Leek, Staffordshire  (NGR SJ 97727 56939). The aims of this assessment were to summarise the character and  extent of any identified features of the historic environment, indicate their significance, the  impact of the proposed development and identify mitigation measures, where appropriate.  The town of Leek has a long held connection with the industrial production of silk, dyes and  textiles. Many of the mills were located adjacent to the area which this assessment addresses,  and with good reason. The site is traversed by the River Churnet which has been used, and  its course modified for agricultural and industrial purposes, since medieval times. The monks  of Dieulacres Abbey resided to the north of the site from as early as the 13th century. They  maintained two mills through the medieval period, the exact location of which are unknown,  although two were recorded during the Reformation in 1538-40 off Mill Street. In the 1740s,  the river's course was manipulated to provide power to the corn mill built by the prominent  canal engineer, James Brindley.A leat of probable post-medieval date crosses the site and is considered to be of importance  to the town's industrial history. At the southeast entrance to the Churnet Industrial Estate a  stone footbridge of 17th-18th century date straddles the river. A further 18th-19th century  industrial site, to the south of the assessment area, is recorded as a mineral works,  associated with the extractive industry, and survives as a brick-vaulted, rock cut chamber.  There are a number of listed buildings adjacent to the site, most notably the mid 18th century  Brindley Corn Mill, within the mill complex which is a scheduled ancient monument.  Consideration will therefore need to be given to the visual setting of these structures which  lie close to the proposed residential area.

title: Historic Building Investigation Cloughbank Farm, Wilmslow Old Road, Altrincham, Trafford
description:
Following consultation with the Greater Manchester Archaeological Advisory Service
(GMAAS), in their capacity of archaeological advisors to Trafford Council, it was agreed
that an appropriate scheme of archaeological works would comprise an historic building
survey. It was recommended that the survey should be consistent with an Historic
England Level 3-type historic building investigation to provide a detailed record of
Cloughbank Farm prior to any alterations or removal of historic fabric. In September 2019, Salford Archaeology was commissioned by Anderton Gables Ltd to
undertake the recommended investigation and fulfil the archaeological planning
obligations. This revealed that a substantial amount of the original seventeenth-century
timber-framed structure survived, and that it represented a relatively high-status
structure, with jettied gables, projecting windows, and a large inglenook fireplace within
the western room of the baffle entry, two-unit house. A further timber-framed wing was
added to produce an L-shaped plan shortly afterwards, with the whole structure being
brick clad, possibly around the time of the addition of a southern wing in the eighteenth
century. The earlier phases suggest that the owner had greater wealth than could be
produced solely by farming, suggesting that he may have been involved with the early
textile trade that was taking off in the local area, particularly the silk trade centred on
Macclesfield. Later additions related to its use as a farmhouse.
Several farm buildings survived, but all date from the early nineteenth century onwards.
The earliest structure represents a fine example of a lowland combination barn, built for
the housing of cattle and the threshing and storage of grain and fodder. Two singlestorey ranges were added to provide further shelter for cattle and a probable pigsty, that
was converted subsequently to a stable.

title: Essex and Suffolk Water Offices, Hall Street, Chelmsford, Essex. Archaeological desk-based assessment
description: An archaeological desk-based assessment confirmed that the site lies within the area of Roman Chelmsford, and reconstructed its topography from previous excavations on adjacent sites and small-scale trenching on the site itself in 1985. The assessment identified a Roman road crossing the north of the site, dating from the late 1st to 4th centuries. Potentially Roman buildings may survive, although only external areas are known for certain. The Roman strata is sealed by a medieval and post-medieval cultivated soil. The standing buildings on the site include the pumping house of the original 1854 water works, and a silk mill built in 1858 and converted by Marconi in 1899 into the world's first radio electronics factory. The assessment recommended trial pit recording to confirm deposit survival, and retention of the industrial standing buildings.
